methodological_rigor.justification: The manuscript aggregates a large multi-study cfMeDIP-seq dataset (1,074 profiles across 9 studies) and applies a uniform processing/QC workflow (MEDIPIPE with 21 QC metrics) to reduce technical heterogeneity. Batch correction and normalization are explicitly described (ComBat-seq followed by DESeq2), with empirical comparisons of alternative approaches and dedicated analyses of SE versus PE sequencing effects. They define discovery features (for example 14,202 pan-cancer DMRs) and include an independent validation set of 220 samples, including cancer types not present in the primary dataset, supporting generalization claims. Key limitations include missing covariates (age/sex missing for >240 samples, leading to exclusion from analyses) and the inherent confounding/label-shift risks of collating heterogeneous retrospective cohorts.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The work is a cross-cohort case–control style diagnostic-development analysis (cancer vs healthy controls and multi-cancer classification with independent validation) rather than a randomized intervention, consistent with Oxford LoE 3b. Clinical relevance is high because the primary aim is minimally invasive multi-cancer detection and classification using cfDNA methylation and fragmentomic features, with explicit external validation in 220 independent samples. The manuscript also addresses real-world implementation barriers (small cohorts and inconsistent processing) by proposing a standardized workflow and a reusable 1,294-sample resource.

reporting_quality.justification: This is primarily a diagnostic/classification study, so STARD is the closest listed reporting frame for reporting diagnostic accuracy and validation. Methods provide detailed preprocessing/QC, normalization, and confounder handling (for example exclusion of sex-chromosome bins after PCA showed sex effects on chrX; exclusion of ENCODE blacklist regions), and clearly distinguish discovery versus independent validation cohorts (220 samples). The reference list includes a public dataset deposition (“pan_cancer_cfMeDIP_Figures_source_data” on Zenodo), supporting a relatively strong data-availability posture in the provided text. Some STARD items (for example prospective recruitment flow, preregistered analysis plans) are not evident in the normalized manuscript and may be incomplete given the retrospective multi-study design.

novelty_literature.justification: The main novelty is the scale and harmonization of a pan-cancer cfMeDIP-seq compendium (1,294 total samples) with an explicit uniform processing strategy to mitigate batch and biological confounding across studies. Integrating methylome markers (pan-cancer DMRs) with fragmentomic features (motifs, fragment lengths, nucleosome footprints) for improved detection/classification is a meaningful methodological extension beyond single-modality approaches. The resource-plus-workflow contribution appears broader than incremental model tuning because it enables reuse and benchmarking across cancer types.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract clearly states dataset composition (1,074 discovery profiles across 9 studies; 220-sample independent validation) and the two feature families (methylome and fragmentome) used for detection. Methods are technically specific, naming pipelines and statistical tools (MEDIPIPE, ComBat-seq, DESeq2) and describing concrete steps taken to address confounding and batch effects. The narrative is dense but generally well structured around harmonization, feature discovery, integration, and validation.

key_strengths: Large multi-study resource (1,294 cfDNA methylomes/fragmentomes) with explicit harmonized processing and QC.
Clear separation of discovery and independent validation (220 samples), including validation cancers absent from the primary dataset.
Thoughtful handling of technical confounding (ComBat-seq+DESeq2 comparisons; SE vs PE effects; exclusion of sex chromosomes after chrX PCA differences).
key_concerns: Retrospective aggregation across heterogeneous studies leaves residual confounding and label-shift risks that are hard to fully resolve.
Missing demographic covariates (age/sex missing for >240 samples) may bias performance estimates and limits subgroup analyses.
Some diagnostic-study reporting items (for example prospective flow diagrams, prespecified thresholds across cohorts) are not obvious in the normalized text.
chief_reviewer.rationale: High-quality computational/biomarker resource work with strong validation and practical value for multi-cancer detection; best placed in a high-impact translational/omics venue, with minor revisions to clarify residual confounding and reporting completeness.
